item.title: Exit Tickets
item.description:
Exit Tickets

A short in-class response that closes each meeting: credit-based, low-stakes, one for every class day (42 across the semester). Credit means completion, not correctness, but you need to be in class to earn it; a ticket completed without attendance gets no credit for that day.

Exit tickets are completed on D2L and due by 5pm the day of class.

Exit tickets do double duty: they tell me what landed and what didn’t before the next class, and they give you a running record of your own thinking to draw on when you write your weekly forum post.

item.title: Forum Posts
item.description:
Forum Posts

Each week there’s outside material to read, watch, or listen to. You respond to a posed question about that material in a roughly 250-word post, using evidence from the material and your own research, cited in APA format. This is also the main place you’ll do the metacognitive analysis described in the learning goals: how your own use of, and relationship to, these systems is shifting.

Forum posts are due on D2L before the first day of class each week (Sunday at 11:59pm).

item.title: Case Studies & Template
item.description:
Case Studies

Most weeks begin with a particular AI‑in‑society use case presented by the instructor. In class, your group (3–4 students) analyzes the case using the DTPA framework, answering key questions with evidence. Early on, groups focus on one component of DTPA at a time (Data → Tools → Practices); later, groups apply the full framework and are expected to locate additional, related cases (e.g., voting, criminal‑justice, environment) to synthesize across uses.

item.title: Lesson Planning & Leading Class
item.description:
Lesson Planning & Leading Class

After the first few weeks of class, groups of students (3–4) can opt in to plan and lead a lesson. Expect this to take each student roughly 10 hours to plan and lead. This is a deeper engagement option, not a requirement.

How to sign up

  • Reach out to your instructor at least one week before your planned lesson
  • A student may only participate once
  • Scheduling depends on availability — your lesson may land later in the semester than requested

What’s expected

  • Learning goals for the session
  • Engagement strategies
  • An appropriate Exit Ticket for your lesson

📌 See the syllabus for how leading a class factors into your Class Engagement grade.

item.title: Case Design & Template
item.description:
Case Design

  • Students: Teams of 3-4
  • Framework: Data-Tools-Practices-Actions (DTPA)

The Case Design project is the principal assessment for the course. Your team develops one case, in stages, over the whole semester. Your chosen topic must be substantial enough in scope to warrant a group effort.

Unlike Case Studies, this is not three separate documents. It is one document that grows: your Final Case Design is a direct expansion of your Scaffold 2, which is a direct expansion of your Scaffold 1. Each scaffold gets instructor feedback, and the next scaffold must respond to that feedback in a separate document.

item.title: Schedule
item.description:
Schedule — Fall 2026

  • Meets: Monday / Wednesday / Friday
  • First class: Monday, August 31, 2026
  • Last class: Friday, December 11, 2026

📌 This is a planning skeleton. Every date is fixed; topics are placeholders (_TBD_) until the reading list and use-case sequence are set.

How a Week Works

This will be our pacing after the first few weeks.

Day Role What happens
Monday Concept Unpack the mechanics behind the week's prep reading — the logic of the machine. What is this system? What can it do? What can't it?
Wednesday Case Take a real deployment through the DTPA framework: Data → Tools → Practices → Actions. Evidence-driven, from primary and secondary sources.
Friday Studio Team work on the design project. Peer review, milestone progress, applying STS resources and ethical frameworks to your own proposal.

Every class day: an exit ticket for credit — a short in-class response that closes the day and seeds Friday’s studio and the weekly reflection.

item.title: Syllabus
item.description:
Syllabus

AI in the Real World: Data, Power, & Society is a general education course that explores the conceptual foundations and societal implications of artificial intelligence. The course is designed to provide students with a critical understanding of how AI technologies are developed, deployed, and experienced in various social contexts. No programming experience is required, but students should be comfortable with basic computer literacy and have an interest in exploring the intersection of technology and society.

item.title: Weekly Readings
item.description:
Weekly Readings

Each week has a prep reading to complete before Monday’s class. Monday’s Concept session assumes you’ve done it — we unpack and argue with the reading rather than summarize it.

📌 The reading list is being built. See the schedule for the week-by-week structure and dates.

What each week’s reading page will include

  • The reading itself — with an honest time estimate
  • Why this reading — what it does for the week’s Concept and Case days
  • Prep questions — what to hold in mind while reading, not a comprehension quiz
  • Going further — optional sources for teams whose project touches this material

How readings connect to everything else

Reading feeds… How
Monday — Concept The mechanics you’ll unpack in class
Wednesday — Case Evidence and vocabulary for the DTPA walkthrough
Exit tickets Daily responses draw on the week’s reading
Weekly reflection Your D2L post should engage the reading specifically
Project Readings double as source material for your team’s evidence base

📌 Accessibility: Readings are selected for availability and diverse perspectives, and provided in multiple formats. If you need an alternative format, contact your instructor — no explanation needed.

item.title: AI and the Real World: Data, Power, & Society
item.description:
AI in the Real World: Data, Power, & Society

The above image was generated by Google Gemini EDU using the course summary to create a banner.

📘 Course Description

This course explores the complex interplay between artificial intelligence (AI) and modern society. Students examine AI’s applications, limitations, and implications across ethics, policy, economics, employment, and justice.

Through readings, case studies, and case designs, we critically analyze how these technologies influence and are influenced by our decisions and interactions. We will trace the uses of these technologies at various times and in various domains, including education, healthcare, and criminal justice, and consider their impacts on individuals and communities.

item.title: CMSE 101: Learning Goals
item.description:
Learning Goals

🦉 The Philosophy

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is not just a technical shift; it represents a fundamental restructuring of labor, power, and knowledge. Most MSU graduates will not be training AI models, but it is likely that they will be working alongside them. The suite of technologies that we call AI (e.g., machine learning, deep learning, generative AI) are not going back in the box, but we will eventually determine stable use cases for this tech.
